Culture & Climate · Week 10 · Oct 5–9, 2026

Routines That Follow Through

From Morning Spark to Ember, make the next action clear and follow through with feedback, repair, and recognition.

This week: clear starts and transitions, Monday–Thursday Morning Meeting, daily DBRC feedback, LiveSchool recognition, and PIT Day preparation.

THE COMMITMENT

It started with a shared commitment

That commitment shows up in the routines students can count on. Begin with a visible task, keep materials within reach, and make the first direction clear before students enter. At each transition, scan for who has started, recognize the action you want repeated, and redirect privately when needed.

This week’s commitment

Start ready. Stay present. Close with care. Use Morning Spark at arrival, a clear First Five at each instructional start, and Ember to keep students engaged and regulated through dismissal. Before students leave, check that devices are returned to their assigned places and that students wait for the adult-directed release.

When a student stalls, use CAR: Clarity—is the next action explicit? Access—are the task and materials available? Regulation—what support helps the student rejoin? Keep the expectation clear and adjust the adult move.

MORNING MEETING

The 15-Minute Neuro-Regulated Morning Circle

Morning Meeting runs Monday through Thursday. Use the provided slides and lesson content so students encounter the same language and practice across classrooms. Keep the routine consistent while strengthening how students engage with the lesson. Connect each practice to a choice students can use later in class or during a transition.

RegulateOrientConnectPracticeCommitTransition

In the Practice phase, use See It → Name It → Do It: show the expectation, ask students to identify what makes it successful, then have them rehearse it. Use CAR to give each student a clear, accessible, regulated way to participate.

Teacher move

Open the grade-band lesson before students arrive. Review the facilitator notes, prepare one action for students to practice, and close by naming where they will use it that day.

DBRC

Feedback that follows through

The daily rating is most useful when a student hears what happened and what to try next. Give feedback during the class or setting you taught, then enter that rating in Emergent Tree. Each instructor submits the rating for their own class. Mentors use the completed ratings for check-ins and pattern review.

One student, four classes

ELA enters ELA; Math enters Math; Science enters Science; Social Studies enters Social Studies. Ground the score in an observable action and tell the student what it means. For example: “You had your materials ready and started after the first direction. That was Responsible.”

Paper trackers are optional. They can help students see progress, but they do not replace digital entries. If access, class assignments, mentors, or the roster look wrong, flag the issue promptly so feedback follows the student across the day.

When a student needs more support, use the grade-specific rubric and Reset + Repair Plan below. Document what happened, connect the student to the appropriate adult, and make the return to learning clear.

Student rubrics · RK–K through Grade 8

CULTURE CORNER

Clarity from the first five to the final transition

Make the First Five clear at every instructional start: where students go, what they need, the first action, what happens when they finish, and where the work belongs. At the end of the day, use the same clarity for Ember, materials, devices, and dismissal.

What the walkthrough looks for

Task visible and readable before entry; assigned seats and materials accessible; students starting without waiting for another explanation; teacher scanning and giving specific feedback. If a start stalls, determine whether the next adjustment is in Clarity, Access, or Regulation.

The prompt supports the routine; adult presence and reinforcement teach it. Choose one small change to rehearse after feedback, then look for students starting with fewer prompts the next day.

Continue using the existing expectation resources and See It → Name It → Do It practice.

STUDENT CULTURE IN ACTION

When IGrow Up

I build what comes next.

On their visit to The Match High School and Career Center, eighth graders put words to the futures they imagine: cardiologist, engineer, entrepreneur, welder, and more. Then they got to work together—visualizing a bridge, making design choices, testing ideas with their hands, and seeing the different shapes a shared challenge can take.

The most compelling part was the thinking between steps: one student holding a piece steady while another adjusted it; a group looking at its design and deciding what to try next. “When I grow up” became something students could practice in the present—imagining, building, listening, and revising with a team.

Students also explored an individual work booth and saw a demonstration of how its sound-dampening design can create a quieter workspace without disrupting people nearby. It offered another way to picture what a working environment could feel like.

LIVESCHOOL

Recognition students can use

The LiveSchool Store will be open Tuesday–Thursday, October 6–8, during lunch. Keep giving immediate, specific points for safe, respectful, and responsible choices. Counselors will have reward menus available in the cafeteria so students can plan before visiting the store.

When a student gives you a reward card, honor a classroom reward within a few days or pass the card to the adult who owns it. The current LiveSchool reward menu lists point values and owners. Continue to recognize the actions that make the First Five, transitions, and Ember work.

Culture is not built in a day. It is built one interaction at a time.
